text: Planning's done — this is the first video where SQL Server Management Studio actually opens. We're standing up Riverside_Staging, the landing zone where each night's raw export lands exactly as it arrives, before anything gets cleaned or validated.

Staging exists to separate "data arrived" from "data is trustworthy." Every column lands as permissive NVARCHAR, nullable, no foreign keys, no real constraints — the whole point is accepting whatever actually showed up, so validation happens deliberately later, not by the database engine silently rejecting a load at 2am.

Every staged row also gets metadata that never existed in the source file at all — a load_id, a load timestamp, the exact source file name. Without that, answering "which load produced this row" after the fact is nearly impossible, and that question comes up constantly once this thing is live.

We also build the error and logging tables planned last video right now — load_errors, etl_run_log, and a load_batch table that generates tonight's load_id. Nothing downstream gets built until this logging foundation actually exists.

Then we prove the permissiveness is real: insert an obviously bad value, a letter where a number should be, and confirm it lands successfully in staging instead of erroring out. That's not a bug — that's the entire design goal of this table.

Nothing user-facing has changed yet. But this is the foundation the warehouse, the SSIS packages, and every troubleshooting lesson later in this series all get built on top of. Next: the dimension tables themselves.
